extracted.intended_audience: architects, designers, and art-historians interested in Venetian/incrusted (Byzantine) architecture and ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive design and evaluative principles for the Venetian 'incrusted' (Byzantine-derived) architectural style as exemplified by St. Mark's: materials, shaft treatment, ornament depth, color usage, and compositional honesty. Useful for architects, conservators, and critics assessing or producing such work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of color as a prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: The perception of color is a gift; the very first requisite for true judgment of St. Mark's is the perfection of that color-faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reader (or critic) 'does not care for color' they cannot form any valid judgment of St. Mark's. Appreciation of color is foundational: the building's claims rest on its value as 'a piece of perfect and unchangeable coloring.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Law I — Plinths and binding cornices to be light and delicate
rubrics_metrics.description: That the plinths and cornices used for binding the armor are to be light and delicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covering pieces must have a certain thickness (at least two or three inches) to prevent fracture and allow for wear; weight of the armor must not be trusted to cement — pieces must be connected to the mass they protect by binding cornices and string-courses and mutually support each other (rivetings only auxiliary). Binding plinths/string-courses must not be proportioned so as to appear to take important load-bearing work or be mistaken for the great cornices/plinths of solid construction; they should be visibly incapable of severer work than assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law II — Abandon science of inner structure (simple, massive inner body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science of inner structure is to be abandoned: the body of the structure, being of inferior and comparatively incoherent materials, should not attempt to express higher refinements of construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inner mass should be solid walls and massive piers assuring sufficiency and strength; finer structural expression should be confined to subordinate parts or directed to support the external 'mail' (where otherwise it might appear dangerously independent of inner material). The external appearance depends on the decorative outer skin rather than inner structural refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law III — All shafts are to be solid (one block, not incrusted)
rubrics_metrics.description: All shafts are to be solid; whatever appears solid must be so in fact, and no shaft shall ever be incrusted or jointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shafts must not be mere incrustations; they should be built of one block (never jointed), both because their virtue depends on consolidation and because cutting and adjusting an incrusted coat is more labor than worth. The Venetian, with access to rich materials, must provide flawless stone shafts. Joints in shafts deceive the spectator's confidence and must be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shafts as expression of wealth — honesty of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts should visibly express the wealth and sacrifice invested: they are like 'large jewels' whose mass and polish demonstrate value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the spectator can visually measure a shaft's mass, shafts must be genuine single blocks of precious stone rather than imitated by joints or thin sheets. Attempting to incrust or joint shafts is a deception comparable to introducing a false stone among jewellery and undermines confidence in the building's expression of wealth and sacrifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law IV — Shafts may be independent of construction (decorative independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The shafts may sometimes be independent of the construction: their chief end can be purely to display beauty rather than sustain mechanical necessities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large 'jewel' shafts may be placed where their real service is nominal; avoid embedding or crowding that conceals surface or reduces their display. Symmetrical or scientific arrangements of pillars are to be regarded as errors in this style; shafts can be sited for best visual effect (to catch sunshine and show polished surfaces) even if structurally redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law V — Shafts may be of variable size (avoid enforced symmetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The shafts may be of variable size; perfect symmetry among shafts should not generally be expected and often indicates wasteful cutting down of better material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because value depends on bulk and stone availability is limited, enforced symmetry (cutting larger shafts down to match smaller ones) is undesirable except in special, costly cases (e.g., baldacchino, shrine). Expect variation of sizes and irregular, rhythmical arrangements rather than rigid equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of jewellery principles for veining and honesty (matching plates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply jewellery methods to stone panels: when veining is beautiful, divide the stone into thin plates and reverse one to create perfectly symmetrical figures, and set corresponding edges in contact to display common origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This both displays the beauty of veining and demonstrates the builder's 'honesty of intention' — similar veining declared by placing pieces edge-to-edge. Avoid disguising similarity (which would be deceitful); honest display allows the spectator to recognize that pieces come from the same block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law VI — Decoration must be shallow in cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: The decoration must be shallow in cutting: thin covering slabs do not admit deep carving and ornament cannot be more than an inch deep at the utmost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculpture on thin slabs becomes a work of fine drawing rather than deep modelling: chisel must not strike hard nor mind be impetuous. This condition compels a different spirit from Northern solid sculpture: expect linear bas-relief, delicate pencilling, and caution in execution. Deep cutting that breaks through the thin covering is forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptural subject selection — favor floral and lower organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Because sculpture is reduced to slight outline, dependence on human form as an ornament is diminished; flowers and lower animals are more intelligible and satisfactory subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shallow relief favors decorative floral/foliate motifs and lower organisms over noble human forms, which lose dignity when reduced to line. The incrusted style will therefore commonly present small, subordinate human figures and abundant vegetal/fantastic ornament derived from Roman traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of surface sculpture — purity and completeness of line
rubrics_metrics.description: Where ornament is linear and shallow the outline will be composed with exquisite grace: there will be no line which could be taken away without injury nor any that could be added with advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandoning naturalism and subordinating form to architectural service leads to designs where every line is necessary; avoid extraneous detail or attempts at full portraiture. The ornamental arrangement must atone for lack of depth by perfect, complete linear composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of drilled hollows/black inlay for contrast and light admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Where safe, the sculptor should leave hollows behind covering slabs or pierce them with holes to obtain points of intense blackness to contrast with the light tracing of the design (and also to admit light to the interior while excluding rain and wind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This artifice creates darkness to refresh the eye in areas otherwise light and pale; deep drill-holes or inlaid black portions may be used more extensively as both an ornament and practical means of admitting light to interiors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color as primary constituent of beauty in incrusted style
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly in proportion as the force of sculpture is subdued, the importance attached to color as a means of effect or constituent of beauty increases; the incrusted style is the only one in which perfect and permanent chromatic decoration is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural colored stones (marbles, porphyry, jasper, alabaster) and permanent materials (mosaic, gilding) to produce subtle tints and harmonies; color should be studied and applied with the precision and honesty of a true chromatic system rather than as mere descriptive paint. Color must be used both internally and externally; the building may function as a 'vast illuminated missal' written in enamel and gold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law VII — Impression not dependent on size (concentrate detail proximally)
rubrics_metrics.description: The impression of the architecture is not to be dependent on size: delicate surface design, color, material preciousness, and legendary interest are independent of large scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because fine sculpture and subtle color cannot be appreciated at distance, the best work must be concentrated within comparatively small spaces so the viewer may examine details closely. Large, cliff-like masses of the North are inappropriate; prefer low walls and shafts whose capitals are near enough to touch.
